## /guides/how-do-image-to-video
URL: https://www.aivideosugc.com/guides/how-do-image-to-video

Image to Video: bring one product photo to life

Upload a single product photo and add a short prompt — watch the photo come alive as a moving product clip, ready for ads and social posts.

The photo supplies the look: colours, surface, background. You supply the action in one short sentence. The camera drift, the pace, how firmly the product keeps its shape: the model decides. That is why the photo matters more than wording.
Upload, describe, confirm, compare: the loop is short and it repeats. Slow down on the first two, since a clean photo and one verb do more than any rewrite. If your product exists only as a page link, start with [URL to Video](/guides/how-do-url-to-video).

Steps:
- Upload the product photo in Home: Home is where a new product starts, so upload the photo there first. A clear shot such as a canvas tote bag on a wooden table works better than a busy scene, because the tool needs the item's edges and color to read. Once the upload finishes you see the photo attached, and the next click takes you to the tool tab you chose from the tools menu.
- Pick Image to Video in the tool tab: The tool tab opens with that photo already attached, and the prompt field sits in front of you. This is the point to decide which of the three documented directions you want, because each one sets a different tone for the prompt you write next. The format controls and the estimate area stay on the same screen, so nothing is hidden behind a second page.
- Write the motion prompt in the composer: In the composer, describe the motion in plain words: a slow push toward the tote, a hand lifting it from the table, a turn that shows the other side. Name the light you want and keep the original framing as the base shot. Set the aspect to 9:16 and the duration to 10 seconds when you are aiming at one of the documented placements.
- Confirm the credit estimate: The confirmation dialog shows the credit estimate before anything is rendered. Read the number, check the aspect and duration once more, then confirm to reserve the credits. A failed job returns those credits automatically, so a misfire does not eat the budget. If something looks off, close the dialog and fix it in the composer before you confirm.
- Compare the clip with your photo: Generation runs and the clip lands in the job view. Play it beside the original photo and compare shape, color and any logo, so the item still reads as the same product. If a detail drifted, open Regenerate, which prefills the composer from the job so you change one line instead of rewriting the whole brief.
- Download the file from the Library: Finished clips sit in the Library next to your drafts and versions, and they stay downloadable for 15 days. Open the job, download the file, and note that the download carries no watermark. For a second platform, use Regenerate to prefill the composer from this job, adjust the prompt, then confirm the new estimate before you render again.

### What a single photo can do
Image to Video suits products that read as one object: a balm tin, a tumbler, a folded shirt. The photo holds still while the model moves around it, so what you sell stays recognisable as motion arrives.
Some jobs want another tool. A page link is faster through URL to Video, which imports listing photos. Several angles in one longer story belong in AI Video, which takes up to four photos. A product that needs a speaker belongs in [AI Avatar](/guides/how-do-ai-avatar).

### What makes a photo workable
The composer accepts up to four product reference photos, and one is usually enough. The model needs a subject it can separate from its surroundings, so it moves the camera without smearing your product's edges.
Plain backgrounds win. A crowded shelf makes the model guess which shape is yours; a wall removes the guess. Even light keeps the label readable. A phone photo counts, since motion comes from your sentence, and the [product photo field guide](/guides/product-photo-tips) covers lighting in depth.

### The quote before the job runs
Before anything runs, the composer shows the cost. A 15-second clip costs 20 credits, a 30-second clip costs 40, and the figure changes with the duration. Set the length first, then read the line.
Choosing between them is a placement question. Fifteen seconds carries one beat for half the credits, which suits a test of a new angle. Thirty buys a second beat, a close-up then a use, if something real goes there.
The confirmation modal restates the estimated cost and your balance. Confirming holds the credits, and a failed job returns them automatically. The job runs on the server, so you can leave the page.

### Reading the motion you got
Watch the clip twice. First with sound off, as a scroller would meet it; then with your attention on the product. One pass says whether the motion reads, the other whether the label survived.
One motion per clip keeps results clean. Two actions in one brief, pick up and pour, split the model's attention and land neither. When a story needs both beats, make two clips and keep the stronger take.
When a result is close but wrong, a variation beats a rewrite. Change one thing, the verb, the photo or the duration, then compare both takes. Two changes at once hide which one fixed it.

### Where the clip goes next
Finished videos wait in the Library, where All videos, In progress, Failed and Completed separate running jobs from ready ones. The badge updates while you are away. Download what you keep within 15 days.
The details modal lists the duration, aspect ratio and resolution you submitted, plus every reference you attached. If the clip needs words, [Subtitle Studio](/guides/how-do-subtitle-studio) works on completed videos and saves each pass as a version. Run the [review checklist](/blog/text-to-video-tutorial-brief-the-ai-video-agent) first.

### How one product photo becomes a clip for any platform
Image to Video starts from a still you already have. Upload one product photo, describe the motion you want in a short prompt, and the tool returns a moving clip that keeps the product readable. You don't book a shoot or hire anyone to hold the item, so a photo taken on a kitchen table can open an ad. When you want to try it, [open the workspace](/app/create).
Three directions are documented for the same photo. A creator-style TikTok unboxing opens on a strong hook and walks through the product, an Instagram get-ready reel sits in soft light with minimal captions, and a Facebook offer testimonial leads with the deal and shows the item in use. All three are 9:16 vertical, 10-second loops. Review the generated details against the photo before you publish, and if you only have a link, [import the product page instead](/guides/how-do-url-to-video).

Note: Good to know — If the action feels wrong but the framing is right, change the verb before the photo. Rewriting one word costs less than reshooting and isolates the cause of a miss.

Checklist:
- Product fully in frame on a plain or blurred background.
- One verb in the action line, no second beat.
- Duration chosen before you read the cost line.
- Confirmation modal cost and balance matching what you expect.
- Clip watched once with sound off before you download it.

Questions:
- What kind of photo works best? One clear product, a plain background and even light. A phone photo is enough, since motion comes from the action you write rather than the source file.
- How long can the clip be? Choose 15 or 30 seconds when you set up the job. The composer shows 20 credits for fifteen seconds and 40 for thirty. Start short when testing a new angle.
- Can I use the clip in ads? Yes. Download the finished file from the Library with no watermark, then use it on your product page, in social posts and in paid ads. Publishing to TikTok or Meta takes one click.
- What happens if the motion comes out wrong? Regenerate with one change: a clearer verb, a cleaner photo or the other duration. Two takes show which input caused the miss. If a job fails, the reason is in plain language and the credits return automatically.

- Photos that survive motion: https://www.aivideosugc.com/guides/product-photo-tips
- The guide, chapter by chapter: https://www.aivideosugc.com/guides/workspace-guide

Next step: Start with the photo you already have — Upload one product photo, write one action, and read the cost before you confirm. A 15-second clip costs 20 credits.

## /guides/how-do-product-links
URL: https://www.aivideosugc.com/guides/how-do-product-links

Product Links: build a product library from your links

Paste product pages once, keep a clean library of every product you sell, and brief videos or images straight from a product card — no re-uploading photos.

Import once, then generate many. The same card works next month: press "Create your video" and the product details and photos travel into the panel, so the fifth ad costs an edit rather than a search through old export files.
The library becomes the working memory of your shop. Corrections you make on a card stay there, retired items leave the shelf, and a tidy set of cards turns each later brief into a quick choice instead of a guess.

Steps:
- Paste the link on Home: Open Home and put the address of a public product page into the link field, for example a listing for a canvas tote. The import reads the page and fills the product with a photo and the details it finds. You can upload a photo instead when there is no page to link.
- Check the imported product: On the same screen, look over the photo and the details the import returned, and fix anything that is off before you go further. A wrong size, a missing color or a short description is edited by hand in the composer, and you can swap the photo for one of your own.
- Confirm the estimate and generate: The credit estimate shows up in the confirmation dialog before anything is charged, so read it against the job you described. Confirming reserves those credits, and if the render fails they come back automatically so you can try again. If the product is not right yet, save the draft, which generates nothing and spends no credits.
- Keep the confirmed page in the library: Confirming stores the product page with its photo and details, which is what makes the second job faster than the first. That saved entry is not tied to one video, so the same listing can serve a short ad today and a longer cut next month. Open the tool tab again and the product is already there to choose.
- Reuse the saved product next time: Start the next video from the saved item in the product library instead of a link. Choose the product, check that the photo still matches what you ship, and brief the new angle in the composer, for example a short vertical cut for a story ad. If the creative already ran, import the advertising results and compare the two versions side by side.
- Find the finished file in the Library: Finished videos and their drafts and versions stay together in the Library, so you can download the file you need without hunting through the composer. Downloads carry no watermark, and the file stays available for 15 days. If a version is nearly right, regenerate from the same job so one detail changes instead of the whole brief.

### The library behind every brief
A card is not a file dump. Each entry holds one product: a thumbnail you recognise, the description the import read, and the host it came from, which is how you spot a card pulled from the wrong shop.
Not every job needs a card. If you will brief one page once and never again, send it straight through [URL to Video](/guides/how-do-url-to-video). Where no product page exists yet, [AI Video](/guides/how-do-ai-video) builds the ad from photos you already own.
Growth is the real test of a library. Two hundred unnamed cards help nobody; twenty you can still describe make a month of briefs feel short, so delete what you have stopped selling.

### What makes a good import
The import needs a public HTTPS product page: your own shop, a marketplace listing, or a landing page. It reads the title, description and images already published there, and a price when the page shows one.
Strong input looks like a shop page: several photos of one item, a description naming material or size, and a price. A thin page produces a card you finish by hand, and [product photo tips](/guides/product-photo-tips) show which frames are worth keeping.

### From card to running job
The scrape preview tells you what to trust. It shows the sourced title, description, detected images and a possible price, each with a confidence label, and a possible price is never treated as confirmed.
Press "Create your video" on the card and the panel opens inline with the product attached. Set duration and aspect ratio for your placement, then read the estimate before you confirm: 20 credits for 15 seconds, 40 for 30 seconds. [Ad sizes by platform](/guides/ad-sizes-by-platform) lists the common ones.
Confirming holds the credits, and the modal restates the estimated cost and your current balance. The banner reads "Generating your video", then "Your video is ready", with Download and Open Library buttons.

### Fixing a card that reads wrong
Open the card before you brief it and check what the brief depends on: photos that show the item, a description you would use, the correct source host. Where the scrape fell short, backfill by hand, and what you save is what later briefs use.
When the product page itself changes, re-import the same URL. New photography or rewritten copy belongs on the card, and nothing moves until you import again, so the library never changes behind your back.

### After the banner says ready
A finished video waits in the Library for 15 days, then expires. Download what you want to keep, or publish to TikTok or Meta in one click; a download carries no watermark.
Captions and on-screen text come later, in [Subtitle Studio](/guides/how-do-subtitle-studio), which works on completed videos only. Each operation saves a new version, the original stays untouched, and versions stack as tabs over the player.
The card stays useful after that. Keep it current, and the next ad starts from work you already did, one click from the shelf you keep tidy rather than a folder you rebuild.

### How the product library saves and reuses a product link
A product link only becomes useful when the page behind it is kept. Every product page you confirm is stored with its photo and details, so the listing you imported once is ready for the next brief. Pull it up from the saved list, check the photo still matches the product you ship, and skip the paste step entirely. The [product link guide](/guides/how-do-url-to-video) covers what the import pulls in from a public page.
Your saved products do more than save typing. Import advertising results and compare the creatives side by side, so the version that worked is easy to spot. Share brand profiles and reviewed product facts with the people who brief the work, and decide who on the team can open them. Everything you keep sits in the [Library](/app/create/library) with your drafts, versions and finished files.

Note: Good to know — Re-import is the fix for a changed page, not for a changed card. If you only want a different lead photo or shorter copy, edit the card directly, and keep the URL for the day the shop rewrites the page.

Checklist:
- One card per product, for items you still sell
- Product photos on the card show the item alone
- Description names the material, size or colour you sell
- Source host points at the shop you use
- Dead products deleted rather than left to clutter the shelf

Questions:
- Which product pages can I import from? Any public HTTPS product page works: your own shop, a marketplace listing or a landing page. The import reads the photos and description already on the page, and blocked pages return a specific reason.
- Can I fix things after the import? Yes. Open the card and backfill what the scrape missed: a photo, a description that skipped the material, or a source host pointing at the wrong shop. What you save is what future briefs use.
- What happens when my product page changes? Import the URL again and the card picks up the new photography and copy. Nothing in your library changes until you do, so a card never rewrites itself between briefs.

- Turn one product link into an ad: https://www.aivideosugc.com/guides/how-do-url-to-video
- Photo tips for small product teams: https://www.aivideosugc.com/guides/product-photo-tips
- The guide, chapter by chapter: https://www.aivideosugc.com/guides/workspace-guide

Next step: Give every product one card — Paste the page you sell most and brief the next ad from the card instead of a folder of photos.

## /guides/how-do-subtitle-studio
URL: https://www.aivideosugc.com/guides/how-do-subtitle-studio

Subtitle Studio: subtitle a finished video in minutes

Pick a finished video, choose the operation, and style the captions with a live preview — then burn in a new version, ready for silent autoplay feeds.

Most feeds play with the sound off, so the caption line is often the only thing a viewer reads before scrolling. A silent autoplay feed turns spoken words into on-screen text. A clip that opens with a line nobody can hear has no argument.
You can caption the speech in the video, or set your own words for each screen. Either way you choose the look, check the sample preview, and keep both cuts. The steps below cover the operations, the style choices, and how to pick the better version.

Steps:
- Open Subtitle Studio from the tool menu: Open [the workspace](/app/create/home) and choose Subtitle Studio from the tool menu, where it sits with AI Avatar, Product Links and the rest of the tools. The subtitle tab opens on a list of your finished videos, because a caption needs a voiceover to read from. Pick one you've already generated rather than a draft.
- Pick the render that carries the voiceover: In the Subtitle Studio tab, choose the finished video, the one whose voiceover you want turned into text. It helps to know the name you gave it when you generated the render, so you can spot it among the versions you've kept. The panel fills with caption lines taken from that voiceover, in the order they're spoken. The footage itself doesn't change at this point.
- Read each caption line and edit it: In the panel, go through the caption lines one at a time. The text is pulled from the voiceover automatically, so most lines only need a glance, but a product name or a number can come out wrong. Fix the canvas tote where the take blurred it, or a price that came through wrong. Every line can be edited before export.
- Set style, size, position and color: Now shape the look. Style offers Classic, Bold or Minimal; size runs S, M and L; position is Bottom, Middle or Top; color is adjustable. Middle tends to sit over a product held in someone's hands, so look at the frame before you settle on it. Keep the words clear of faces and fine product detail, and choose a color that separates from the background rather than blending into it.
- Check the frame before you export: Play the captioned video once through in the tool tab and watch the words, not the product. Check the lines you rewrote and the ones near a face, where a caption is hardest to read. If something sits badly, change the position or the color in the panel and play it again. When the clip reads cleanly, you're ready to export.
- Export, then find the new version in Library: Export writes the captioned file as a new version, so nothing you already had is overwritten. The original render stays where it was, and the captioned cut appears beside it. Open [the Library](/app/create/library) from the workspace and check both are there, then download the captioned version before the 15 days run out. Finished files are kept for 15 days without a watermark.

### Captions carry a silent feed
A muted feed removes your voice track and leaves the picture. Viewers still decide within a second whether the clip is for them, and words on screen are the fastest thing to read. Captions turn a spoken line into a visible claim.
Reach for this tool when the footage is settled and the words need work. If the shots are wrong, go back to the composer: the [AI Video guide](/guides/how-do-ai-video) covers a fresh render. Captions repair a silent cut, not a dull one.

### What each operation asks of you
Generate subtitles reads the speech in the video and turns it into captions, so you bring nothing but the finished clip. Promo lines and Product copy take text you write, each line becoming one screen. A pasted paragraph arrives as one crowded line.
Good input is short. Write one idea per line, each short enough to read in a breath. Three tight lines beat a full script, and [the AI UGC video ads guide](/blog/ai-video-tutorial-write-product-ad-prompts-that-work) shows how an opening works.

### Preview, then save a version
Pick the video from the list on the left, narrowing it with a word from the prompt or the title. Choose the operation, then set Style, Size, Position, Colour and Backdrop. The sample caption preview updates as you change each control.
Starting the job saves a new version instead of overwriting the file you selected. The original keeps its Library entry and the captioned cut arrives beside it. Leave the page while the job runs; the badge updates when you return.

### A caption that runs past the screen
A line is too long when the preview wraps or reaches the edges before the sentence ends. On a phone the limit is how often the eye jumps back to the start, not the character count. If reading it aloud leaves you behind, the line is long.
Three clean repairs: cut the line to its subject and verb, split it across two screens, or raise Size a step and drop it to the bottom. Change one thing, then watch the preview. Style combinations that hold up stay legible over moving footage.

### Comparing versions before you post
Versions stack as tabs above the player. Switch between them at the same timestamp, sound off, and ask which answers a buyer's first question. A line that reads well on a desktop can vanish into a busy phone frame, so check the crop you will post.
Keep the tab you trust, download it, and publish. Finished videos stay in the Library for 15 days, so download what you want to keep. Crops for each placement sit in [ad sizes by platform](/guides/ad-sizes-by-platform), with [the review checklist](/blog/text-to-video-tutorial-brief-the-ai-video-agent) for the rest.

### Style, size and position for every caption
Caption work comes last in Subtitle Studio, after the video itself is generated. You don't write the text: it's read from your voiceover automatically, line by line. Your job is the look and the wording. Pick a style, a size, a position and a color that stay readable over the product, then read each line against what's on screen. Open the tool from the menu in the workspace and the settings below are what you see.
Nothing about the video's picture changes — you're only adding words on top. The captioned file is saved as a new version, so the render you already had stays in the Library untouched. Every line can be edited before you export, which matters when a product name or a price has to be exact. Read through the lines, fix the ones that came through wrong, then export.

Note: Good to know — Copy written for reading lands better than copy written for speaking: cut the filler and let the picture carry the rest. Two versions are enough; a third makes choosing harder.

Checklist:
- The video you open is completed, not still running.
- Each on-screen line fits one screen in the preview.
- Style, Size and Backdrop were checked on the busiest frame.
- Both versions were watched muted at the same timestamp.
- The chosen version is downloaded before the 15 days end.

Questions:
- Will the original video change? No. Every operation saves a new version, and the video you picked keeps its own entry in the Library. Versions stack as tabs over the player, so the first cut stays available.
- What can a new version contain? The operations are Generate subtitles, Promo lines and Product copy. Generate subtitles captions the speech already in the video; the other two set your own words, one line per screen. Captions keep the language of the audio.
- Which style reads best on mobile? Bold type with a box or outline backdrop in the bottom third is the safest start, because it survives busy footage and pale backgrounds. Check the preview at Medium before going larger. Middle suits one short line.
- How long do the versions stay? Finished videos sit in the Library for 15 days, then expire, versions included. Download the cut you plan to post and keep your own copy of anything you reuse.

Next:
- Give the captions a presenter: https://www.aivideosugc.com/guides/how-do-ai-avatar
- Review a cut before it goes live: https://www.aivideosugc.com/blog/text-to-video-tutorial-brief-the-ai-video-agent
- The guide, chapter by chapter: https://www.aivideosugc.com/guides/workspace-guide

Next step: Caption the cut you already approved — Open Subtitle Studio, pick a finished video, and keep both versions until one reads better on a phone.

## /guides/how-do-text-to-video
URL: https://www.aivideosugc.com/guides/how-do-text-to-video

Text to Video: from one sentence to a video brief

Type one sentence about your product. AI writes the script and scenes, and turns it into an editable video brief — then generates the shots you choose.

Nothing renders while you read that brief. Every line stays editable, from the opening shot to the closing words, and the price appears once you settle on a version. Most first drafts need one pass to sharpen the claim and one to cut a repeating shot.
Reach for this tool when you have a product and a point to make, but no script. If photos or a product page already exist, a sibling tool saves the typing.

Steps:
- Start the product in Home: Home is where a new product begins, so open it first and add the canvas tote: paste the product link if the page exists, or upload the photo if it does not. Confirm the product, then choose Text to Video from the tools menu. The tool tab opens with that product attached, and the composer is the next thing you see.
- Write one plain line in the composer: In the composer, describe the product the way you would to a friend rather than in prompt language: a heavy canvas tote on a wooden table in warm afternoon light, a hand pulling out a green water bottle. One line is enough to start. Leave the tool, model, aspect, duration and resolution as they are for now, then click Optimize and read what comes back.
- Read the six lines the optimizer returns: The composer answers with six labeled lines, from the look and the light to the sound and the rules. Each one is a working instruction, so compare the framing and the lighting with the tote in your hand. If the voiceover or the shot order is off, fix it there in place rather than retype the brief.
- Edit the row that needs work: Every row stays editable. Change the light in the style line, cut a shot from the list, or add a rule such as keep the print sharp when the label matters. Keep the edits short, because the prompt is what the clips are built from. Read the whole prompt once more after a change, so two lines do not ask for opposite things.
- Confirm the estimate in the dialog: The estimate sits on the same screen as the format controls, and the confirmation dialog shows it before anything runs. Compare the number with the duration and the count of shots, and shorten the clip if it reads high. Confirming reserves the credits for this job, and a job that fails returns them automatically.
- Collect the file from the Library: When the render finishes, open the Library and find the job among your drafts, versions and finished files. Play it once at full size and check the print, the bottle and the light against the real tote. Then download the file, which carries no watermark and stays available for 15 days. If a detail drifted, Regenerate prefills the composer from the job so you change one line.

### Where a sentence beats a photo
Text to Video suits a claim you can say out loud: a serum that calms redness, a mat that stays put through a sprint. The brief supplies the shot order, the on-screen words and the voice. Photos can ground the scenes, but they never replace the sentence.
Pick a different tab when the raw material already exists. [AI Video](/guides/how-do-ai-video) starts from one to four product photos and keeps the item in frame; [URL to Video](/guides/how-do-url-to-video) reads a public HTTPS product page and builds the brief from it. AI Image returns stills inline.

### The sentence that starts everything
Name three things in one or two lines: the product, the person you are talking to, and the single message they should leave with. A line carrying all three gives the composer a structure to fill. A slogan gives it nothing.
Compare "Give this moisturizer an honest review" with "Great results, amazing product". The first names an item, a tone and a job. The second could sit under any product on any shelf, so the scenes come back generic.

### What you set before the quote
Five controls decide what you pay for and what comes back: the Type selector, then model, aspect ratio, duration and resolution. Set them before you press Optimize, because each one shapes the brief the composer writes.
Then the quote. The confirmation window restates the estimated cost and your balance, and confirming holds the credits while the job runs. A failed job returns them automatically, with a plain-language reason and a Try again button. Save as draft costs nothing if the brief can wait.

### Judging the result shot by shot
Open the details modal for the finished video, the per-shot clips, the description, every reference you attached, and the submitted duration, aspect ratio and resolution. The per-shot clips show which scene missed, instead of letting the whole edit take the blame.
Separate the two kinds of failure before you spend anything. Retry render re-runs assembly while the existing clips stay untouched, which fits footage that is fine and joins that are not. Regenerate prefills the composer from the job, so rewrite the weak scene and keep the rest.

### Where the file goes next
Completed videos land in the Library under four filters: All videos, In progress, Failed and Completed. They stay for 15 days and then expire, so download the version you want to keep.
Captions come later, in [Subtitle Studio](/guides/how-do-subtitle-studio), and only for completed videos. Generate subtitles reads the actual speech, Promo lines and Product copy write on-screen text from your own words, and each operation stacks a new version over the player.
Publishing is one click to TikTok or Meta, or a download with no watermark. Keep the first paid clip narrow, one claim and one duration, so the next version has something honest to compare against. For the account side, see [the first TikTok video ad](/guides/first-tiktok-video-ad).

### How the prompt optimizer builds a scene-by-scene script
Open [the workspace](/app/create) and pick Text to Video from the tools menu. In the composer you type one line of plain words, such as a canvas tote on a wooden table in afternoon light, then tap Optimize. The editor answers with a scene-by-scene prompt that carries framing, lighting and sound. Tool, model, aspect, duration and resolution sit on the same screen, so the brief and the format stay together.
Nothing in the prompt is locked. You can rewrite any of the six lines, from the light and the shot list to the rules about on-screen text, before anything renders. The credit estimate appears before you confirm, and confirming reserves those credits, while a job that fails hands them back. If you already hold good product photos, [Image to Video](/guides/how-do-image-to-video) is the shorter route.

Note: Good to know — A guest can build and save a draft without an account, and the draft is restored when the guest signs in. Drafts cost nothing, so you can rewrite the sentence as often as the claim changes.

Checklist:
- The sentence names the product, the audience and one claim.
- Every scene has a shot you can picture.
- Aspect ratio and duration match where the video will run.
- The quoted credits match the length you need.
- You opened the per-shot clips before rerunning the job.

Questions:
- How long should the first sentence be? One or two lines. Name the product, the one thing it does and who you are talking to. The composer expands that into scenes and voice, so length matters less than having a single claim to land.
- Can I edit the script before generating? Yes. The brief is fully editable: reorder scenes, rewrite lines, drop a shot. You confirm only the version you want to render, and the quote you approve belongs to that version.
- What happens if a job fails? You see a plain-language reason and a Try again button, and the held credits return automatically. There is no support ticket to file and no charge for the attempt.

Next:
- Make a video from product photos: https://www.aivideosugc.com/guides/how-do-ai-video
- Check a clip before you publish it: https://www.aivideosugc.com/blog/text-to-video-tutorial-brief-the-ai-video-agent
- The guide, chapter by chapter: https://www.aivideosugc.com/guides/workspace-guide

Next step: Write the sentence, then read the quote — Type one line about your product, press Optimize, and edit the brief until the claim reads right. Credits are held only when you confirm.

## /guides/how-do-url-to-video
URL: https://www.aivideosugc.com/guides/how-do-url-to-video

URL to Video: turn a product link into a video ad

Paste one product URL — AI imports the photos and details for you, then turns them into a ready-to-post video. No camera, no filming, no editing timeline.

The path suits a listing already good enough to sell from. If the photos are the weak part, improve them first. The importer can only work with what the page shows, so a thin listing produces a thin draft.
Nothing about the import is fixed in place. You correct the copy, choose the photo the video opens on, and describe the demo in your words. Building the draft costs nothing; the price of the video appears after you review it.

Steps:
- Paste the product link: Open [Home](/app/create/home) and paste the link to the product page into the field at the top. Use a public product page rather than a private account screen, so the import can read it. Once the link is in, you continue in the tool tab, where the import begins and the photos and copy start to fill in.
- Review what the import found: In the tool tab, the import lists the photos it found, often a plain product shot, a model shot and an in-use shot. Below them sit the title, the description, the detected price and the product details. Read each one against the real product and note anything that looks wrong, such as a color name or a price that no longer matches the page.
- Correct the details by hand: Move to the composer and edit the fields the import left thin. If the page carried no size, type the tote measurements or a short line such as heavy canvas with two handles. Rewrite the title in plain words and trim the description to two sentences. Save the draft when the fields read right, since saving generates nothing and spends no credits.
- Brief the video in the composer: The import has already written a first draft, so read it before you change it. Keep the shot order if it makes sense, then rewrite the lines that describe the product: what appears in the first three seconds, the scene, the framing and the sound. Adjust the duration and the aspect ratio on the same screen, and leave the draft saved if you want to stop here.
- Confirm the estimate and generate: The composer shows the credit estimate before anything runs. Read it next to the duration and the shot count, then open the confirmation dialog. Confirming reserves the credits for this job. If the number looks high, step back and cut a shot or shorten the duration before you confirm. A job that fails returns its credits automatically, so you can try again.
- Collect the file from the Library: When the render finishes, open [the Library](/app/create/library) and find the job under your finished files. Play it once at full size before you download, checking the product photo against the real tote. Download the file and post it, or send it to Subtitle Studio first if you want captions. The file stays downloadable for 15 days and carries no watermark.

### Where the link path saves time
A working product page already answers what a script has to answer: what the item is, who it suits, and why a buyer would choose it. The importer turns those answers into the first draft, so you review instead of compose.
Take a different start when the page is not the bottleneck. A single strong shot moves faster through [Image to Video](/guides/how-do-image-to-video), and a product with no page yet belongs in [Text to Video](/guides/how-do-text-to-video). Sellers planning many videos keep every import in [Product Links](/guides/how-do-product-links) instead.

### What the importer needs from the page
The link must be public and served over https. Pages behind a login, a cart gate or a regional block do not open for the reader, and the tool returns a specific reason rather than a blank draft. That reason tells you what to fix.
Good input is a listing a stranger could buy from: a clear title, a description with real detail, and photos large enough to survive a vertical crop. One thumbnail and a single line of copy give the draft almost nothing to shape.

### Checking what the import read
The preview returns four things: the sourced title, the description, the images it detected, and a possible price. Each carries a confidence label, so you can tell a clean read from a guess. Read all four before you brief anything.
A possible price stays a hint and is never treated as confirmed. The reader may pick up a sale price, a variant price or a shipping line, and nothing checks it. If the ad shows a number, type the one you stand behind.

### Confirming cost and starting the job
One click on the imported entry opens the prefilled draft in the composer, with the photos, the description and the format settings already in place. Add a sentence of direction, then read the estimate.
A 15-second video costs 20 credits and a 30-second video costs 40. The confirmation modal restates that cost and your balance; confirming holds the credits. A failed job returns them, and the job runs on the server.

### Where the finished video goes
Finished work lands in the Library under All videos, In progress, Failed and Completed. The details modal shows the result, the per-shot clips, the description, every reference you attached, and the submitted duration, aspect ratio and resolution.
When one clip is wrong, pick the smallest repair. Try again re-runs a failed job, Retry render re-assembles clips that are already fine, and Regenerate prefills the composer from the job. Captions are a separate pass in [Subtitle Studio](/guides/how-do-subtitle-studio), and each pass saves a new version.

### How to import a product page into your first draft
Start at your workspace Home and paste the link to a public product page. The import reads that link and usually brings back a main product shot, a model shot and an in-use shot, plus the title, the description, the detected price and the product details. It also writes a first draft of the video, so you start with a structure rather than a blank brief.
Nothing is charged until you have read what the import returned. The imported photos and fields land in the tool tab, where you can fix anything the page did not carry, such as a size, a color name or a short description. Once the brief reads right, the credit estimate appears before you confirm, and confirming reserves those credits. A job that fails hands them back.

Note: Good to know — Guests can build the draft without an account, and it is restored the moment they sign in. Save as draft costs nothing, so compare two directions before spending credits.

Checklist:
- The product page opens in a browser without signing in.
- The description on the page matches what you actually sell.
- You chose the shot the video opens on, not the first one listed.
- The price in the copy is one you typed, not the imported guess.
- You read the estimate before confirming, not after.

Questions:
- Does the product page need anything special? It needs to be public and served over https. The reader takes the title, the description, the photos and a possible price from the page. A page behind a login returns a specific reason instead of a draft.
- What if the import picks a photo I don't want? Deselect it before you brief the video, then choose the shot the video opens on from the ones you keep. The video is built only from those photos. A wide lifestyle image often crops down to an empty frame.
- How much does one video cost? The composer shows the estimated credits before anything runs. A 15-second video costs 20 credits and a 30-second video costs 40, and the confirmation modal restates the cost and your balance. A failed job returns the credits.
- What happens to the price the importer found? It stays a possible price, marked with a confidence label, and it is never treated as confirmed. The reader can pick up a sale price, a variant price or a shipping line. Type the figure you want in the ad.

## /guides/product-photo-tips
URL: https://www.aivideosugc.com/guides/product-photo-tips

AI Product Image Generator Tips From Your Phone

Your shop's AI product photo generator can start with how you take the photo: your phone and window light. A plain gray running shoe can then sit on a white board, or in a room you name, without a studio day.

### Put Your Product in a New Setting
The same product can sit somewhere new, and it stays the product you ship. Your photo is the start.
A bright outdoor setting can make the product feel ready for sun or travel. Check that the color still matches in daylight.
A dry, open place gives the product a surface that feels rugged. Watch the shadows so the edges stay clear.
A plain light background is the safest listing look, and a good start when you are unsure.
A room you can name puts the product where a shopper already lives. One sentence can say the product, the surface, and the light.

### Benefits of AI Product Photos
You skip the studio day once the phone photo is done. The product in the file stays the product you ship.
You spend less than a studio, a stylist, and a model for every color of the same product.
A listing photo can start after you close for the day, with no studio date on the calendar.
A long catalog can share one setup across many products. Each image is its own job. You do not open a second app.
A hand can hold the product on a surface you already have. Use an AI actor as the presenter. The [actor library](/ai-actors) is where you choose.
Late hours use the same plan you already pay for. The generator is there whenever you are packing orders.
You can see the product on a plain background in one file and in a room in another. Run those two as separate ads and keep the one people watch.

### How to Make an AI Product Photo in 3 Simple Steps
Upload a sharp photo and name the setting. Download after you check the color, with no studio day.
Upload your product photo, or describe the picture in one plain line. Keep the whole product sharp.
Rest the phone so it stays still. Use the volume button or a short timer when the shutter fires.
Fill most of the picture and leave a slim margin. Step closer instead of pinching to zoom.
Set the product beside a window in bright, indirect daylight, and turn the ceiling lights off.
Warm bulbs mixed with daylight shift the color, and that shift shows up in later images too.
A plain board, a gray card, or bare wood is enough behind the product. Wipe dust before you shoot.
Hold the phone level with the product, and keep every edge inside the picture.
Turn off portrait mode, filters, and beauty settings. They blur the background and change the color.
Tap the product to lock focus. If white areas lose all detail, lower the brightness until you see the texture.
Take a side, a three-quarter view, and any other side the listing needs. Each one needs its own photo.
Upload only a side the photo actually showed. Zoom until the edges are clear, and compare the color in daylight.
Upload the original file, not a screenshot. JPG, JPEG, PNG, WebP, BMP, TIF, TIFF, HEIC, and HEIF work. The limit is 32 MB.
Describe the scene in one sentence: the product, the surface, and the light. Save the price for your own editor.
Download and check the real product beside the screen. Fix the color or the edges with a follow-up sentence if needed.
Open a lifestyle photo, a new background, or a white background when the listing needs a different file.
The same still can start [AI image to video](/ai-video-generation/image-to-video) when the listing also needs a short video.

### Product Photo Examples From One Shot
List the same product in a new place, using only details that were in your photo.
Try a bright outdoor table, with the side that faced the camera.
Try a bench in early light, with the parts a shopper needs to read still easy to see.
Show a side only when your photo showed that side. Then try a three-quarter view from its own photo.
Show the product on bare wood, the whole item in frame, with a simple room behind it.
Use a plain light board, with daylight from the side, and keep the full shape in frame.
Try a low angle only at the size your photo showed.
Try a clean side view, with every edge inside the picture.
Try a desk only when the source photo showed the parts you want in frame.
Keep the color the same as the item you sell, with nothing smoothed away.
Lay the product on its side only if that side was in the source photo.
Use a front view only when the source photo showed the front.

### How Shops Use These Product Photos
A shop puts the product on a bright bench and in a bag shot, with the edges still clear.
A home seller starts from a phone photo and gets a clean tabletop without renting a studio.
A gift shop shows the product on a wood shelf, from a photo of the item alone.
A fitness shop makes a morning scene and an evening scene from the same photo.
A small catalog lays the product flat, then asks for a plain background and a street setting.
A shop keeps the shape readable and adds the price later in its own editor.
A store tries a living-room floor and a patio before it picks a listing image.
A launch week uses the new photo on the product page the week that item goes live.
A shop shoots the sides first, so later images keep the parts that were in the photo.
A small team makes the listing photo, then a short [product video](/ai-video-generation/product-video) with a voiceover or captions.

### One Photo, Ready to List
You get a listing photo when the shape is clear and the color is true. Shoot at product height, in window light, with filters off. Then pick a place and match the new image to the real item.
Each image is 1 credit, shown before the job starts. Starter is $24 for one month with 200 credits, Pro is $59 for 500, and Studio is $129 for 1,200. If a job fails, the credits come back. Downloads have no watermark.

Questions:
- Are these photos useful on a product page? Yes. Use a clear product image on your listing, then make another scene for ads or social posts. The photos have no watermark.
- Do I need a camera, or is a phone enough? A phone photo is enough if it is clear and well lit. Show the whole product so the new image keeps its shape and details.
- How much does an AI product photo cost? One product photo costs 1 credit. Starter costs $24 for one month with 200 credits, Pro costs $59 for 500, and Studio costs $129 for 1,200.
- What should I look for before I publish? Check the color, shape, and small details against the product you sell. Clear, realistic photos help shoppers decide with confidence.
- Can I sell with these photos? Yes. Use watermark-free product photos on your store and in paid ads. Make sure you have rights to the image you upload.
- What do I gain from an AI product photo? You get realistic product images quickly without renting a studio. Try different backgrounds and lighting to see what suits your store.
- How does the product photo get made? Upload a product photo and describe the scene you want. The tool makes a new image with your product, lighting, and background in minutes.

## /guides/testing-ad-versions
URL: https://www.aivideosugc.com/guides/testing-ad-versions

AI Video Ads Generator for Ad Tests

Use this AI video ads generator to test one change at a time, so you learn which opening people actually watch. Make a few versions and run them together.

### How the AI Video Ads Generator Works
It makes a short ad from your product, a prompt, or a link. A script, a presenter, and a voice come with it. You do not film, and you do not need a crew.
Each file is made for the shapes paid platforms expect. Keep the audience and the budget the same so the test stays fair.

### How to Compare Ad Versions
You can compare openings because the photo, the length, and the shape stay the same. Change only how the clip starts.
One version can open on the product in hand. Another can open on the product in use. Keep the photo and the line the same.

### Why Test Ad Versions
Script the ad from the real product page, so the hook matches what you actually sell.
Match the file to the screen. Use 9:16, 1:1, 16:9, 4:3, or 3:4 for TikTok, Facebook, Instagram, and YouTube.
When the test is about who is on screen, keep the product photo and the opening, and change only the person.

### How to Make a Test Ad in 3 Simple Steps
Upload Your Product Photo. Add one clear photo of the product. That photo is in every file, with no extra filming day.
You describe the opening; the tool drafts the hook and script, then adds an AI actor, voice, and edit.
Download and Post. You get a file with the opening you named. Read the line, and keep the file when the product in the picture is the one you ship.
Download the shape this test is using. A square for a feed and a tall file for a phone are two separate tests.
Each clip is its own file. A video is 20 credits for 15 seconds or 40 for 30. You see the cost before you start. If a file does not finish, the credits come back. Keep the captions and the music the same on every file. When one version gets a different headline above the ad, you are testing that headline too. [AI image to video](/ai-video-generation/image-to-video) makes another clip from that photo. [URL to video](/ai-video-generation/url-to-video) makes one from the product page. Pick the AI actor from [the actor library](/ai-actors).

### Benefits of AI Video Ads for Tests
The next version is another file from the photo you already sent. Change one thing, so a new opening does not wait on a shoot.
You pay one-time package credits instead of per-video creator fees: Starter starts at $24 for one month with 200 credits.
One photo can open in more than one way. Keep the product the same, and keep the length the same, across those files.
When people start to scroll past an ad, retire that file. The next file changes the first second and keeps the price the same.
You decide what the line is allowed to claim. If the product page names a fact, the line can name that fact. The photo still has to show your product.
You can use the download in ads and on your store. It has no watermark. The version that wins can run as a paid ad.

### Tools for the Next Ad Test
The next tool still uses the product you are already testing.
[Video ads](/ai-video-generation/video-ads) makes a phone-style clip. [Image to video](/ai-video-generation/image-to-video) is for when you already have the photo. [URL to video](/ai-video-generation/url-to-video) is for when you start from the product page. [The actor library](/ai-actors) is for when you are testing the presenter. [Ad images](/ai-image-generation/social-ad-photos) is for when the version is a photo. [Templates](/templates) is for when you want a layout that is already set.

### AI Video Ads vs a Filming Day
Turnaround: you get a version from a photo or a link, while a filming day waits on a person, a place, and a date.
Cost: a filming day bills the day, the person on camera, and the editing after. A version here draws on the plan you already pay for. Starter is $24 for one month with 200 credits.
Variants: each extra opening is another file from the photo you already have. The product stays the same.
Brand control: you write the line, using the facts on the product page. A hired person has to follow that written line.
Usage rights: the file can sit on the product page and in a paid placement. Ask a hired creator, in writing, where their film is allowed to run.
A shop with many products can reuse one opening on each item that has its own photo. Each item is still its own file.

### How Shops Set Up One Test
Run three openings of the same product, and change only the first second. The product stays the product in the photo.
Make one clip from the photo you already have. Do not build a second set.
Keep the same product, and change only the first second between the two files.
If you sell in another country, change the spoken language and keep the same product. The script names only what the product page says.

### How to Keep a Small Test Fair
Change only one thing between versions, so the result points at that one thing.
Worth testing, one at a time: the opening, the setting, the shape, the length, and the line you add afterward. Start with the opening. It decides whether anyone sees the rest.

### How the Versions Should Run Together
One campaign gives every version the same audience, the same budget, and the same product page.
Many ad accounts let several ads share one group. Some also split the audience across versions. A version that barely ran has not been tested. Leave the ads alone while the test is live.

### How to Tell Which Version Works
Wait until each version has actually played before you name a winner.
Read three numbers in order. First, how many people stay past the opening. Second, how often people click. Third, the cost each time someone buys. A version can get more views and still lose on sales.

### What the Next Test Should Change
Keep the version that brings sales at a cost you can accept. Turn off the clear losers, and change one new thing.
Write down the date, what changed, and the result. When a winner starts costing more per sale, make fresh versions. Work through the opening, the setting, the shape, the length, then the offer.

Questions:
- Where do I see which ad version worked? Check your ad account for views, clicks, and sales for each version. The video tool makes the ads; your campaign results show what worked.
- Can Meta or TikTok reject an AI video ad? Yes. An AI ad can be rejected if it breaks the platform’s ad rules. Check claims and any required AI disclosure before you spend more.
- Should I change the price in just one ad version? Keep the same price when you are testing a new opening or visual. Test a different price separately so you know what changed the result.
- How does AI make a video ad? It makes video ads from a product photo, link, or short description. You get a script, presenter, and voice without filming.
- Do I have to label an AI actor in my ad? Follow the platform’s current disclosure rules when you post. Be especially clear if the video could look like a real customer review.
- How many ad versions should I test first? Start with a few versions so each gets enough budget to compare. Change one thing at a time, such as the opening, to see what helps.
- Can I make ads for several products? Yes. Use a photo or link for each product and make versions for your catalog. You can test different products and openings without a new shoot.
- What if one ad version barely gets shown? Give each version enough exposure before comparing results. If one gets almost no views, you cannot tell whether its opening worked.
- Which tool should I use to test video ads? Choose one that makes several versions from the same product and lets you change the opening quickly. AIVideosUGC can make those versions without new shoots.
- Which video sizes can I download for ads? Choose 9:16 for TikTok and Reels, 1:1 for feeds, or 16:9 for wide placements. You can also choose 4:3 or 3:4.
- How much do AI video ads cost? Videos cost 20 or 20 credits depending on length. Starter costs $24 for one month with 200 credits, Pro costs $59 for 500, and Studio costs $129 for 1,200.
- How do I make video ads to test? Start with a product photo or link and make several versions with different openings. Keep the product and offer the same so you can compare results.
- Can I use AI videos as paid ads? Yes. You can use the downloaded video in paid ads without a watermark or separate actor license. Check that your product claims are accurate before posting.
- What should I test first in a video ad? Test the opening first because it decides whether people keep watching. Make several short versions from the same product photo and compare them.
- Do AI video ads work as well as filmed ads? Results depend on your product, audience, and offer. Try both in the same ad account to see which brings more clicks or sales.

## /guides/white-background-amazon
URL: https://www.aivideosugc.com/guides/white-background-amazon

Amazon Main Image Rules for Every Listing

Meet Amazon's main-image rules at catalog scale. One pure-white setup, then send the set to Seller Central.

### A Pure White Main Image for Every Product
Amazon requires a pure white main image. If the corners are not white, the listing can drop out of search until you replace that picture.
Take one backpack photo as an example. Remove the old background, then set the corners to pure white, 255 on red, green, and blue. You do not need a studio for that.
Sale stickers, badges, and extra objects stay off this picture. The product should fill most of the square, and it should be the one you ship.

### Built for a Whole Catalog
A shop with many products can reuse the white square once the first one looks right. Save that setup and apply it to the rest.
Use that same white square as the first photo on your own store too.
You set pure white once, choose how much of the square the product fills, and name what ships in the box. The next product uses that setup.
You confirm shape, color, and label against the item in your hand, and then you publish the file that matches.

### Start From a Phone Photo, Not a Studio
You do not need a white studio. The phone photo needs the whole product, sharp, with even light and a little space around every edge.
Take the photo near a window, on a plain surface, and hold the phone at the product's height. Show what the buyer finds in the box. Flash can blow out the color, so window light is safer.

### Make the Pure White Main Image
Open the [AI product background changer](/ai-image-generation/change-background) or the [AI product photo generator](/ai-image-generation). Ask for the product on pure white, filling most of the square.
Then sample a corner. It should read 255 on red, green, and blue. If it does not, ask again before you upload.

### Use the Same White Setup on Every Product
A white main image keeps a listing easy to find in search. Replace a gray main image and the listing can show in search again. The later photos are not the ones this rule is about.
Once the first square is right, use that same square on the next color. The API is not a separate install. It can start the next file from the catalog you already keep.

### Keep Your Brand on the Later Images
Save your colors and your wordmark for the photos after the main image. Those later photos are where colors and the wordmark belong. The main image stays a clean product on white, with no lettering.
The white square is only the first picture. The product in use, or a hand for scale, belongs in the later spots. [Photos of daily use](/ai-image-generation/lifestyle-photos) and [photos with a person](/ai-image-generation/model-photos) cover those spots.

### How to Make Amazon Listing Photos in 3 Simple Steps
Upload your product photo. Get the main image right on one product before you touch the rest. The square is white, and every piece that ships is in the frame.
Describe your scene for the later pictures. The second picture can show the product in use. Add your colors in the editor only on that later image.
Download and post. When that pair looks right, repeat it for the other products and send the files to Seller Central.

### Use AIVideosUGC or Build It Yourself
A two-person shop can give the product a white main image with the plan it already pays for. You can start today. You do not staff an engineering project first.
The bill you already know is the plan and the credits. That is the cost of the white square, including a quiet month.
When the photo tools improve, that shows up in the product you already open. You do not keep a second image tool running.
A busy season can bring many new colors at once. The white setup from last month still applies. The API is not a separate build.
The colors on a later Amazon photo should match your own store. Set them once. The white main image stays free of lettering.

### How a Catalog Seller Uses the Main Image
Every new product gets the same pure-white main image. Photos of the product in use stay in the later image spots.

### More Photo Tools for the Listing
[Background changer](/ai-image-generation/change-background) takes off the old background. [White background](/ai-image-generation/white-background-photos) is the tool for the main image. [Product photos](/ai-image-generation) cover the rest of the square. [Photos of daily use](/ai-image-generation/lifestyle-photos) belong in the later image spots, not on the main image.

### Check the Product Before You Upload
You upload a file whose corners are full white and whose product matches the one in your hand. Check the corners with a color picker, then set the real item next to the screen.
Each corner should be pure white, with no gray haze. Zoom in on labels, because small lettering is where a new image often goes wrong. If the words are wrong, try again from a sharper phone photo before the file goes to Seller Central.

### When the Product Is White, Clear, or a Set
Set the product's shape first, light the edges, and show exactly how many pieces the listing sells.
Side light keeps a pale product's outline visible on white. Take the starting photo with light from one side, and mention that side light in the line you type. If two pieces ship, both stay in the frame. A clear bottle needs the same edge light, or it can disappear into the white.

### Keep White for the Main Image Only
Only the first picture has to be the white square. Picture two can show the product in use. Picture three can show a detail up close.
Make the pictures first, then add any words in the editor. [Photos of daily use](/ai-image-generation/lifestyle-photos) are for those later spots. A soft shadow, when you want one, stays off the main image.

### Upload the White Square You Checked
A large product, white corners, the right pieces, and a readable label are the file you upload. Check the item in your hand against that file.
The phone photo can start on any plain surface. One finished image is 1 credit, shown before it starts. A failed job returns those credits. Starter is $24 for one month with 200 credits, Pro is $59 for 500, and Studio is $129 for 1,200. The same white setup can repeat across the catalog. The API is not an extra fee.

Questions:
- What if the product is white, clear, or a set? Use side lighting to keep a white or clear product visible against pure white. Include every item in a set that you actually ship.
- Will the product's shape change? The image should keep your product’s original shape and color. Review straps, labels, and edges against your source photo before posting.
- How many credits does one white image use? One white-background image costs 1 credit. Failed jobs return their credits. Starter costs $24 for one month with 200 credits, Pro costs $59 for 500, and Studio costs $129 for 1,200.
- How can I make an Amazon image with a pure white background? Upload a phone photo, remove its background, and choose pure white. Check the product edges and every corner before using it as a main image.
- Can my shop system start the white image? Yes. Your shop software can send product photos through the API and request white-background images. Review the results before adding them to listings.
- Can an image made here be my Amazon main image? Yes, if the image shows the product you sell on pure white without extra props or text. Check Amazon’s current main-image rules before uploading.
- Can I make white-background images for many products? Yes. Apply the same white background and framing to multiple product photos. Review each image so the color, label, and shape still match the item you sell.
- What happens if my Amazon main image breaks the rules? Amazon may suppress a listing with a noncompliant main image. Replace it with a clear product image on pure white, then check that the listing is visible again.
- What are Amazon’s main image requirements? Amazon main images need a pure white background, a clear view of the product, and no extra text or props. Check the current rules for your category before uploading.
- Why does my white background look gray on Amazon? It may be off-white or have a gray shadow near an edge. Check that the background is RGB 255, 255, 255 across the full image.
